newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa's pneumonia to keep her in hospital.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa's pneumonia to keep her in hospital.

text.p: Doctors treating Mother Teresa said on Sunday the 86-year-old nun had suffered a setback in her recovery from pneumonia and they were concerned about her unstable condition.
They said the Roman Catholic missionary was suffering from bronchial pneumonia which had not yet responded to antibiotics or respiratory treatment. She would stay at least another week in hospital.
"There seems to have been some sort of setback," A.K. Chatterjee, an administrator at Calcutta's B.M. Birla Heart Research Centre, told a news conference.

"Her bronchial pneumonia is unchanged, signs of congestion and infection still present," doctors treating the renowned nun said in a regular bulletin on her condition. Earlier they had said they were concerned about her condition.

Mother Teresa underwent surgery on November 29 to clear two blocked coronary arteries. She appeared to be recovering normally, despite an irregular heartbeat, when long-standing lung and kidney problems resurfaced.
The 1979 Nobel peace prize winner also contracted bronchial pneumonia, which doctors have treated with antibiotics. Every six hours they have removed fluid which has collected in her lungs.
They said on Sunday the measures to check the pneumonia had not been as effective as they hoped, but did not say what setback she had suffered.
"Today Mother Teresa appears fatigued but she heard mass sitting on the chair and took a few steps," the bulletin said.
Chatterjee said she met her colleagues in the Missionaries of Charity religious order to discuss administrative matters.
She also walked a distance of about 40 feet (10 metres) in the clinic's intensive care unit supported by two nurses, he said.
On Saturday, doctors delayed a procedure to correct her irregular heartbeat because they wanted to wait until she was stronger.
The procedure, known as cardioversion, involves drugs or a mild electric shock. "It has been put on hold for at least another two days," Chatterjee said.
"Once general conditions improve, cardioversion will be attempted for irregular rhythm," the doctors said.
Chatterjee said there was no chance Mother Teresa would be able to resume her work with the poor and the sick before next weekend. "It will be a miracle if she is released early," he said.
